*My Hypothesis are:
H1: Attitudes toward gender equality differ significantly across gender groups.
  Categorical IV: Sex. Continuous DV: Gender equality composite Composite items: Gender_Equality_1, Gender_Equality_2, Gender_Equality_3.

H2: Individuals reporting greater romantic intimacy with their partners report higher relationship satisfaction.
  Continuous IV: Romantic intimacy composite. Continuous DV: Relationship satisfaction. Composite IV items: Love_1 through Love_15 DV items prqc_1 through prqc_6


```{r library}
library(ggplot2)
library(labelled)
library(codebook)

```


```{r loadingData}

rawData <- read.csv('raw-data/data_doctored.csv')

#Making sure that data exists
dim(rawData)
str(rawData)

```


```{r checkValidity}

finishedCol <- rawData$Finished == 1#Selecting all the finished surveys (discarding non finished ones).
DATA <- data.frame(rawData[finishedCol,])#Filtering the data to have only the finished surveys.


validResponseIdIndex <- !is.na(DATA$ResponseId) # Identify valid ResponseIds
DATA <- DATA[validResponseIdIndex, ] # Filter the dataset

# Verify valid responses
if (sum(is.na(DATA$ResponseId)) == 0) {
  print("Nice, all the responses are valid!")
} else {
  print("There are some NA/NaN responses.")
}
```

```{r duration filtering}
###JK: Fix the duration filter before using the resulting data. ###
# summary(durationFiltered[5]) summarizes the fifth observation, rather than calculating Q3 from all durations. The resulting vector is recycled in the comparison.
# The two row filters are then applied to different versions of DATA, even though both masks were made from the original rows. This produced 1,714 rows with missing IDs after your ID check.
# If you have a reason to use these cutoffs, make one mask from the full duration column and apply it once:
# duration <- DATA$Duration..in.seconds.
# bounds <- quantile(duration, c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE)
# keep <- !is.na(duration) & duration >= bounds[1] / 2 & duration <= bounds[2] * 2
# DATA <- DATA[keep, ]
# State why you chose the cutoffs and report how many rows were removed.
###  End of comment ###

### AC Comments:
# I Revised the code and made the necassary changes. In this new version, I discard less then 10 quantile and more than 90 qunatile entries. This is because, in some responses, response time are unlikely, i.e., 5 second response time for the whole survey is not applicable. Similarly, 10 hours of response time is also not applicable.
##End comments

duration <- DATA$Duration..in.seconds.
bounds <- quantile(duration, c(.10, .90), na.rm = TRUE)
keep <- !is.na(duration) & duration >= bounds[1]  & duration <= bounds[2] 
DATA <- DATA[keep, ]

print(paste0("There are ", length(duration) - length(DATA$Duration..in.seconds.), " rows are deleted"))

durationDistHist <- ggplot(data=DATA,
                       aes(x=Duration..in.seconds.)) + geom_histogram(bins=100) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x="Duration in seconds (LOG Scale)", y="Counts in LOG Scale",title="Survey Response Duration Plot after filtering")

durationDistHist


```



```{r column filtering}
#The row data has 273 columns/variables. I won't be using all of them for my hypothesis.

genderEqList <- list()
for (i in 1:3){
  a <- paste0("Gender_Equality_",i)
  genderEqList[i] <- a
  
}


loveList <- list()
for (i in 1:5){
  a <- paste0("Love_",i)
  loveList[i] <- a
  
}

pqrList <- list()
for (i in 1:6){
  a <- paste0("prqc_",i)
  pqrList[i] <- a
  
}

varNames <- c("ResponseId","Sex", unlist(genderEqList), unlist(loveList), unlist(pqrList))

FDATA <- DATA[varNames] #Filtering data, to select the desired columns. (FDATA == Filtered data)

```



```{r filtering and recoding}
validData <- FDATA

genderListFiltering <- apply(FDATA[, unlist(genderEqList)], 1, function(x) all(!is.na(x) & (x >= 1 & x <= 7)))
loveListFiltering <- apply(FDATA[, unlist(loveList)], 1, function(x) all(!is.na(x) & (x >= 1 & x <= 5)))
prqcListFiltering <- apply(FDATA[, unlist(pqrList)], 1, function(x) all(!is.na(x) & (x >= 1 & x <= 7)))
sexFiltering <- !is.na(FDATA$Sex)

###JK: Make separate datasets for H1 and H2. ###
# H1 needs gender and gender equality. H2 needs the two relationship scores. Combining all four checks removes respondents for missing items unrelated to the hypothesis being tested.
# Keep ResponseId in varNames and export separate H1 and H2 tables. The following is an example to adapt for H1 after you fix the duration step:
# ge <- paste0("Gender_Equality_", 1:3)
# h1 <- DATA[, c("ResponseId", "Sex", ge)]
# for (item in ge) {
#   value <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(trimws(h1[[item]])))
#   h1[[item]] <- ifelse(value %in% 1:7, 8 - value, NA_real_)
# }
# h1$gender_equality <- rowMeans(h1[, ge], na.rm = FALSE)
# h1$Sex <- factor(h1$Sex, levels = 0:3, labels = c("Men", "Women", "Non-binary", "Prefer not to say"))
# h1 <- h1[complete.cases(h1[, c("Sex", "gender_equality")]), c("ResponseId", "Sex", "gender_equality")]
# Use these gender labels in the H1 plot. For H2, apply the 1-5 and 1-7 item checks to the selected Love and PRQC items separately.
###  End of comment ###

# Converting items to numeric
itemNames <- c(unlist(genderEqList), unlist(loveList), unlist(pqrList))

FDATA[itemNames] <- lapply(
  FDATA[itemNames],
  function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(trimws(as.character(x))))
)

genderListFiltering <- apply(FDATA[, unlist(genderEqList)], 1, function(x) all(!is.na(x) & x %in% 1:7))

loveListFiltering <- apply(FDATA[, unlist(loveList)], 1, function(x) all(!is.na(x) & x %in% 1:5))

prqcListFiltering <- apply(FDATA[, unlist(pqrList)], 1, function(x) all(!is.na(x) & x %in% 1:7))

sexFiltering <- !is.na(FDATA$Sex) & FDATA$Sex %in% 0:3


# Separate filtering for H1 and H2 as JK's feedback highlights.
combinedIdxH1 <- genderListFiltering & sexFiltering
combinedIdxH2 <- loveListFiltering & prqcListFiltering

validDataH1 <- FDATA[combinedIdxH1, c("ResponseId", "Sex", unlist(genderEqList))]
validDataH2 <- FDATA[combinedIdxH2, c("ResponseId", unlist(loveList), unlist(pqrList))]


# Reverse-code the gender_equality variables.
validDataH1[unlist(genderEqList)] <- lapply(
  validDataH1[unlist(genderEqList)],
  function(x) 8 - x
)

# Label the gender groups
validDataH1$Sex <- factor(
  validDataH1$Sex,
  levels = 0:3,
  labels = c("Men", "Women", "Non-binary", "Prefer not to say")
)

```

```{r finding averages}

###JK: Match the H2 item sets to the constructs in your hypothesis. ###
# Love_1-15 cover intimacy, passion, and commitment. Use Love_1-5 for intimacy. PRQC_1-3 measure satisfaction, and PRQC_4-6 measure commitment.
# If keeping the current hypothesis, change both item lists before validating and averaging, so eligibility and scoring use the same items:
# loveList <- paste0("Love_", 1:5)
# pqrList <- paste0("prqc_", 1:3)
# If keeping the broader scales, revise the hypothesis and axis labels to match. The plot shows an association, so describe the pattern without saying one score directly affects the other.
# Add var_label() descriptions for the two final tables and use compact_codebook() as in Lab 03. Save the final tables with write.csv(..., row.names = FALSE) for later labs.
###  End of comment ###


validDataH1$avgGenderEq <- rowMeans(validDataH1[,unlist(genderEqList)])
validDataH2$avgLoveIntimacy <- rowMeans(validDataH2[,unlist(loveList)])
validDataH2$avgPrqc <- rowMeans(validDataH2[,unlist(pqrList)])

# Keep the necessary variables for each hypothesis
validDataH1 <- validDataH1[, c("ResponseId", "Sex", "avgGenderEq")]

validDataH2 <- validDataH2[, c("ResponseId", "avgLoveIntimacy", "avgPrqc")]

```

```{r codebook generation and saving new csv files.}

var_label(validDataH1) <- list(
  ResponseId = "Participant response identifier",
  Sex = "Reported gender category",
  avgGenderEq = "Gender equality composite score (1-7)"
)

var_label(validDataH2) <- list(
  ResponseId = "Participant response identifier",
  avgLoveIntimacy = "Romantic intimacy composite score (1-5)",
  avgPrqc = "Relationship satisfaction composite score (1-7)"
)

compact_codebook(validDataH1)
compact_codebook(validDataH2)

#Saving the hyptohesis
write.csv(validDataH1, "processed-data/H1.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(validDataH2, "processed-data/H2.csv", row.names = FALSE)



```


#H1: Attitudes toward gender equality differ significantly across gender groups.
  Categorical IV: Sex. Continuous DV: Gender equality composite Composite items: Gender_Equality_1, Gender_Equality_2, Gender_Equality_3.

```{r plots: H1}

h1Plot <- ggplot(data = validDataH1, aes(x = factor(Sex), y = as.numeric(avgGenderEq), fill=factor(Sex))) +
  labs(
    title = "Gender Equality Attitudes by Sex",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Gender Equality Composite Score"
  ) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_boxplot(width=0.08, box.color="white") +
  labs(title="Gender Equality Attitudes by Sex", x="Sex", y="Gender Equality Composite Attitude Score (1–7)") +
  guides(fill=FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:7, limits = c(1, 7))

pdf(file="plots/h1.pdf")
h1Plot
dev.off()

```

H2: Individuals reporting greater romantic intimacy with their partners report higher relationship satisfaction.
  Continuous IV: Romantic intimacy composite. Continuous DV: Relationship satisfaction. Composite IV items: Love_1 through Love_5 DV items prqc_1 through prqc_6
  
  
```{r plots: H2}

h2Plot <- ggplot(validDataH2, aes(x=avgLoveIntimacy, y=avgPrqc, fill=avgPrqc)) +
  geom_point(alpha=0.1, position=position_jitter(width=0.05, height=0.05)) +
  geom_smooth(method="gam", se=T) +
  labs(
    title = "Romantic Intimacy and Relationship Satisfaction",
    x = "Romantic Intimacy Composite Score (1–5)",
    y = "Relationship Composite Satisfaction Score (1–7)"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  theme_minimal() + guides(fill=F)

pdf(file="plots/h2.pdf")
h2Plot
dev.off()
```

#Comments:

It seems like both of my hypothesis hold. More specifically, for my first hypothesis, I was able to see different attitudes toward gender and equality.

For my second hypothesis, it was clearler to interpret, romantic intimacy directly effects relationship satisfaction.
